prompt: `Wiring.java` runs the bookshop's classes with `@Service` and `@Repository` still on them, and Spring never starts. What did those annotations do in that run?
hint: Who reads an annotation?

choices.text: They started Spring in the background, from the jars on the class path
choices.why: A jar on the class path runs nothing by itself. Nothing called `SpringApplication.run`, so there was no container to start.

choices.text: Nothing, because no code read them
choices.why: An annotation is a label for code that looks for it. `main` never looked, so the classes ran as plain Java and the report still counted three books.

choices.text: They made the compiler write the `new` calls into `main`
choices.why: The compiler copies an annotation into the class file and leaves it there. Every `new` in that run is one you can read in `main`.

choices.text: They stopped `main` from creating a second `BookService`
choices.why: Nothing enforces one instance outside a container. `main` could call `new BookService(...)` twice and get two objects.

prompt: In `Wiring.java`, why does `new BookService(repository)` have to come after `new InMemoryBookRepository()`?
hint: Read `BookService`'s constructor.

choices.text: Spring always creates repositories before services
choices.why: Spring is not running in `Wiring.java`, and in the application no rule ranks stereotypes: the constructors decide the order.

choices.text: The repository has to load its books before the service can be compiled
choices.why: Compiling runs no constructor. The order matters when the program runs, not when it is compiled.

choices.text: Its only constructor takes the repository as an argument
choices.why: An argument has to exist before the call. Spring meets the same constraint and resolves it the same way, dependency first.

choices.text: Otherwise `BookService` would create a repository of its own
choices.why: `BookService` has no code that creates a repository; it stores whatever it is given. With nothing to give, the call would not compile.

prompt: Which of these is inversion of control in the bookshop?
hint: Who calls whom?

choices.text: `BookService` calling `new InMemoryBookRepository()` itself
choices.why: That is the opposite: a class fetching its own dependency, so that nothing outside can choose another.

choices.text: `BookRepository` being an interface rather than a class
choices.why: An interface lets the implementation change. It says nothing about who creates the objects or who calls them.

choices.text: Spring running the constructors in the reverse of their natural order
choices.why: The order is not reversed: a dependency is still built before whatever needs it, as in `Wiring.java`.

choices.text: `CatalogueReport.run` being called by code that is not the bookshop's
choices.why: The report never decides when it runs. Spring Boot calls every `CommandLineRunner` after start-up, and nothing in the bookshop calls `run`.

prompt: Component scanning gives the class `InMemoryBookRepository` the bean name `___`.
hint: The simple name, with one letter changed.

prompt: In the beans log, Spring starts on `bookService` and creates `inMemoryBookRepository` before it finishes `bookService`. Why?
hint: What does `bookService` need before it can exist?

choices.text: `bookService` cannot be built until its constructor argument exists
choices.why: The repository is the argument of `BookService`'s only constructor, so it is created first, when it is needed. The log's next line names it.

choices.text: Spring creates beans in alphabetical order of their names
choices.why: Alphabetically `inMemoryBookRepository` would be last of the six. It was created second, at the moment it was needed.

choices.text: A `@Repository` is created before a `@Service` in every application
choices.why: No rule ranks one stereotype above another. Take away the constructor parameter and nothing would force this order.

choices.text: The first attempt at `bookService` failed and Spring tried again
choices.why: Nothing failed: the log shows one creation of each bean and no error, and the report ran.

prompt: `BookService`'s constructor asks for a `BookRepository`, and the log says it was autowired to the bean `inMemoryBookRepository`. What made Spring choose that bean?
hint: Read the words "by type".

choices.text: Its name matches the parameter
choices.why: The parameter is called `books`, which is no bean's name. A name only breaks a tie, and there was no tie.

choices.text: `BookService` imports `InMemoryBookRepository`
choices.why: It imports nothing of the kind. It mentions only the interface, which is the point of having one.

choices.text: It was the one bean of that type
choices.why: Spring matches a parameter by its type first. One candidate means no decision to make.

choices.text: It was the first `@Repository` found in its package
choices.why: Where a class sits in its package decides nothing. With two candidates Spring would stop rather than take the first.

prompt: Which of these would component scanning in the bookshop turn into a bean? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two conditions: the label, and the package.

choices.text: `ClockConfig`, a `@Configuration` class in `com.example.bookshop.config`
choices.why: `@Configuration` is a stereotype and the package is below `com.example.bookshop`. The log created it as `clockConfig`.

choices.text: A `@Component` class in `com.example.billing`
choices.why: The label is right and the package is not: `com.example.billing` is beside the bookshop's package, not below it.

choices.text: A `@Service` class in `com.example.bookshop.ordering`
choices.why: A stereotype in a package below the application's: both conditions hold. Lesson 14's order service sits exactly there.

choices.text: The interface `BookRepository`
choices.why: An interface cannot be instantiated. It is the type the beans are matched by, not a bean of its own.

choices.text: A class with no annotation in `com.example.bookshop.catalogue`
choices.why: The package is right and the label is missing. Scanning looks for stereotypes, as the deleted `@Repository` line showed.

prompt: Why does `BookService`'s constructor carry no `@Autowired`?
hint: How many constructors does the class have?

choices.text: Spring Framework 7 removed `@Autowired`
choices.why: It still exists; the field-injection detour uses it. It is simply not needed here.

choices.text: `@Service` puts `@Autowired` on every method
choices.why: `@Service` marks the class for scanning and says nothing about its methods or constructors.

choices.text: Records never need it, and `BookService` is one
choices.why: `BookService` is a class with a field and methods. `Book` is the record.

choices.text: It is the class's only constructor
choices.why: With one constructor there is nothing to choose, so Spring uses it. `@Autowired` is needed to pick one of several.

prompt: After `BookService` was switched to field injection, the application still started. What failed, and where?
hint: Two runs: inside Spring, and in `Wiring.java`.

choices.text: Spring refused to write a private field
choices.why: Spring writes private fields by reflection. It did, and the application counted three books.

choices.text: Outside Spring: `new BookService()` left `books` null and `list()` threw
choices.why: Only the container sets the field. Built by hand, the object exists without its dependency until the first call.

choices.text: The compiler rejected the `@Autowired` field in `BookService`
choices.why: `BookService` compiled. What stopped compiling was `Wiring.java`'s call to a constructor that no longer exists.

choices.text: Inside Spring the report counted zero books
choices.why: It counted three: inside Spring the field was set before anything used it.

prompt: A colleague's `PriceService` has eleven constructor parameters, and they propose field injection so that the constructor looks less crowded. What does the switch change?
hint: What was the parameter list telling you?

choices.text: Spring creates fewer beans, since fields are cheaper than parameters
choices.why: Every dependency is still a bean. Only the way it reaches the class changes.

choices.text: It hides the eleven dependencies; the class needs just as many
choices.why: A long parameter list is a sign the class does too much. Field injection removes the sign and keeps the cause, and adds a way to build the object incomplete.

choices.text: The fields can now be `final`, which a constructor did not allow
choices.why: The reverse: a field written after construction cannot be `final`, and a constructor-assigned one can.

choices.text: A missing bean is now reported at start-up, where before it was not
choices.why: Both forms fail at start-up when a bean is missing. Only the constructor form also fails at compile time when somebody builds it by hand.

prompt: When does the bookshop's interface `BookRepository` pay for its extra file?
hint: Spring does not require it.

choices.text: Always, because Spring cannot inject a class that implements no interface
choices.why: A constructor may ask for a class, and Spring injects the bean of that class.

choices.text: Now, because the interface makes the repository safe to share between threads
choices.why: Thread safety comes from `ConcurrentSkipListMap` and `AtomicLong` inside the class. A type cannot provide it.

choices.text: In lesson 9, when a PostgreSQL repository replaces it and `BookService` is untouched
choices.why: That is the second implementation the interface was written for. Without one in sight, an interface is a file and nothing more.

choices.text: Never, since the interface has only one implementation in this lesson
choices.why: One implementation today is not the test; one in view is. Lesson 9's is four lessons away.

prompt: Why is the bookshop's clock defined by a `@Bean` method and not by a stereotype annotation?
hint: Whose class is `Clock`?

choices.text: `Clock` is a JDK class, not one the bookshop wrote
choices.why: A stereotype goes on a class you wrote. For one you did not, a method that returns an instance is the definition.

choices.text: Component scanning skips the `config` package
choices.why: It scanned it: that is how `ClockConfig` itself became the bean `clockConfig`.

choices.text: A `@Bean` method makes the clock a prototype
choices.why: A `@Bean` is a singleton unless it says otherwise; Spring called `clock()` once and kept the result.

choices.text: Stereotype annotations work on interfaces only
choices.why: Every stereotype in the bookshop sits on a class. `Clock` is excluded by who owns it, not by what it is.

prompt: A `@Bean` method declared as `public Clock clock()` defines a bean whose name is `___`.
hint: It comes from the method, not from the type.

prompt: A new `DiscountService` decides whether today is a sale day by calling `LocalDate.now()`. What problem does the bookshop's injected clock avoid that this one has?
hint: Try to write a test for the last day of the sale.

choices.text: `LocalDate.now()` is much slower than reading an injected clock
choices.why: Speed is not the difference. Both read the same system clock in the end.

choices.text: `LocalDate.now()` cannot be called from inside a singleton
choices.why: Any code can call it, from anywhere. That is exactly why nobody can replace what it returns.

choices.text: No caller chooses the day, so a test's result depends on when it runs
choices.why: The date is a hidden input. With a `Clock` parameter, a test passes `Clock.fixed` for the last day of the sale and checks the answer.

choices.text: `LocalDate.now()` returns the date in UTC instead of São Paulo
choices.why: It uses the machine's default zone, which is a second hidden input. The first is that nobody can replace the clock at all.

prompt: A report says: `Parameter 0 of constructor in com.example.bookshop.catalogue.BookService required a single bean, but 2 were found`. What happened?
hint: Parameter 0 is the repository.

choices.text: `BookService` was created twice
choices.why: The report is about the candidates for one parameter. `BookService` was never created at all.

choices.text: `BookService` has two constructors and Spring could not choose
choices.why: It names a parameter of one constructor. A choice between constructors fails with a different message.

choices.text: Two beans have the type that the parameter asks for
choices.why: Two classes implement `BookRepository` and both are beans, so matching by type no longer decides.

choices.text: Two of `BookService`'s parameters have the same type
choices.why: Its constructor has one parameter. The 2 counts beans, not parameters.

prompt: Match each start-up report to the repair that removes its cause.
hint: One right-hand item repairs nothing.

pairs.left: required a single bean, but 2 were found
pairs.right: mark one candidate @Primary, or qualify the parameter

pairs.left: required a bean of type ... that could not be found
pairs.right: give the class a stereotype, in a package under the application's

pairs.left: the dependencies of some of the beans form a cycle
pairs.right: move what both classes need into a third class

prompt: Both `EmptyBookRepository` and `InMemoryBookRepository` are beans. `InMemoryBookRepository` carries `@Primary`, and `BookService`'s parameter carries `@Qualifier("emptyBookRepository")`. What does `BookService` receive?
hint: One is decided by the candidate, one by the consumer.

choices.text: `inMemoryBookRepository`, because `@Primary` overrides any qualifier
choices.why: `@Primary` is the default for consumers that do not say. This one says.

choices.text: Neither: start-up stops with two candidates
choices.why: Each annotation alone settles the tie, so together they cannot reopen it.

choices.text: `emptyBookRepository`, because the qualifier names it
choices.why: A qualifier is the consumer naming exactly the bean it wants, and it wins over `@Primary`.

choices.text: Both, as a list of two repositories
choices.why: Spring injects a list only when the parameter's type is a `List`. This one is a single `BookRepository`.

prompt: Another project has two `PaymentGateway` beans, no `@Primary` and no `@Qualifier`, and still starts. Which explanation fits?
hint: Spring's last tie-breaker.

choices.text: The constructor parameter has the same name as one of the two beans
choices.why: A parameter named like a candidate wins the tie, provided the compiler kept the names. Renaming it would quietly change the wiring.

choices.text: Spring took whichever of the two it found first
choices.why: Spring does not guess between candidates. The bookshop's two repositories stopped start-up with a report.

choices.text: The build no longer passes `-parameters` to the compiler
choices.why: That would remove the names the tie-breaker reads, and the tie would end in the two-candidates report.

choices.text: The two beans are declared in different packages
choices.why: A package decides whether a class is scanned, not which of two scanned beans a parameter receives.

prompt: With `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true`, the constructor cycle between `bookService` and `catalogueReport` still stops start-up. Why?
hint: What would Spring have to hand over first?

choices.text: A property on the command line is ignored when it is about circular references
choices.why: It was read: the report's Action changed to say that the references were allowed and the cycle still could not be broken.

choices.text: Each constructor needs the other object to exist first
choices.why: The property lets Spring pass a half-built object, which needs the object to exist first. A constructor that has not run has built nothing.

choices.text: The property only applies to beans created by `@Bean` methods
choices.why: It applies to any bean injected by field or setter. Constructors are what it cannot help.

choices.text: Spring Boot 4 removed the property and kept only its message
choices.why: The property exists and was honoured; the second report differs from the first because of it.

prompt: In Spring, a bean in the default singleton scope exists once per what?
hint: It is not the design pattern.

choices.text: Per Java virtual machine, guaranteed by the class itself
choices.why: That is the singleton design pattern. `Wiring.java` made a second repository with `new` and nothing objected.

choices.text: Per thread
choices.why: One object is shared by every thread, which is why it has to be safe to share.

choices.text: Per HTTP request
choices.why: That is the request scope, which a web application adds.

choices.text: Per application context
choices.why: The container makes one and hands the same object to everybody who asks it.

prompt: `BookService` is made a prototype and injected into the singleton `ScopeCheck`. How often does `ScopeCheck` receive a new `BookService`?
hint: When does a constructor run?

choices.text: Every time one of its methods uses the field
choices.why: The field holds whatever the constructor was given. Nothing replaces it between calls.

choices.text: Once, when `ScopeCheck` itself is created
choices.why: Injection happens when the constructor runs, and a singleton's constructor runs once. That is the trap of a prototype inside a singleton.

choices.text: Never: a prototype cannot be injected into a singleton
choices.why: It can, and was: the run compared the injected object with the others.

choices.text: Once per HTTP request that reaches the application
choices.why: That would be a request-scoped bean behind a proxy. A prototype has no proxy and no link to requests.

prompt: Why does `InMemoryBookRepository` keep its books in a `ConcurrentSkipListMap` and number them with an `AtomicLong`?
hint: How many objects of it exist, and who calls them?

choices.text: Spring refuses a `@Repository` whose fields are not thread-safe types
choices.why: Spring checks nothing of the sort. Safety is the author's job, which is why the author chose these two.

choices.text: It is a singleton, so one object serves every thread that calls it
choices.why: Two requests can save a book in the same instant. A plain map and counter could then hand out one id twice.

choices.text: To keep the books in alphabetical order of title
choices.why: The map is sorted by its keys, which are the ids. Titles play no part.

choices.text: Because it is a prototype, created again for every request
choices.why: It is a singleton: one object, created once, as the log said. A new object per request would need no protection at all.

prompt: Put what happens when the bookshop starts in order, from the first step to the report.
hint: Definitions before objects, and an argument before what needs it.
items: Component scanning reads com.example.bookshop and the packages below it
A bean definition is collected for each stereotyped class
inMemoryBookRepository is created, because bookService's constructor needs it
bookService is finished with the repository as its argument
trap: Creating bookService before its repository is the order a reader who has not read the constructor expects; Spring cannot, because the constructor has nothing to be called with.

prompt: A new `@Component` class, `ShelfLabelPrinter`, sits in `com.example.printing` and takes a `BookService` in its constructor. The application starts without an error and the printer never does anything. Which explanations fit? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which classes depend on the printer?

choices.text: `com.example.printing` is outside the scanned packages, so no bean was made
choices.why: It is beside `com.example.bookshop`, not below it, so scanning never read the class.

choices.text: A `@Component` needs `@Autowired` on its constructor to be created
choices.why: A single constructor is used without it, as `BookService`'s was.

choices.text: Nothing depends on the printer, so its absence breaks no constructor
choices.why: The "could not be found" report needs a consumer asking for the missing type. With none, a class that is never created fails silently.

choices.text: A `BookService` cannot be injected into a class of another package
choices.why: Injection does not care about packages once a bean exists. `CatalogueReport` and `ClockConfig` live in different ones and meet.

prompt: `BookService` is a prototype. `CatalogueReport` and `ScopeCheck` each take one in their constructors, and `ScopeCheck.run` calls `getBean(BookService.class)` twice. How many `BookService` objects has Spring created by the time that run ends?
hint: Every injection and every `getBean` of a prototype is a new object.

prompt: Which single change to this lesson's code would stop the application at start-up?
hint: A missing bean is an error only when something asks for it.

choices.text: Moving `CatalogueReport` to the package `com.example.reports`
choices.why: It would stop being a bean and stop running, and nothing asks for it, so start-up would succeed without a report.

choices.text: Renaming `BookService`'s parameter from `books` to `repository`
choices.why: With a single candidate, matching by type decides and the name is never consulted.

choices.text: Moving `InMemoryBookRepository` to the package `com.example.storage`
choices.why: No bean of type `BookRepository` would exist, and `BookService`'s constructor asks for one: the "could not be found" report.

choices.text: Adding `@Autowired` to `BookService`'s constructor
choices.why: It is allowed on a single constructor and changes nothing.
